summary.text: 七 is the character for “seven.” Crossed forms are documented writing the numeral from oracle-bone writing onward, though one disputed account proposes that the graph first represented cutting and was later borrowed for “seven.”

formation.text: The formation is disputed. One proposal interprets the crossed graph as depicting a cut across a line, then suggests the sign was borrowed for the numeral because the words may have sounded alike. The competing account documents 七 for “seven” in oracle-bone writing onward; the original referent, spoken name, and proposed sound connection are not established.

history.text: The selected oracle-script-style image shows crossed horizontal and vertical strokes; the seal-style image shows the lower vertical stroke bending to the right. These are modern redrawings, not artifact photographs. A paleographic study reports crossed forms from oracle-bone writing through early Western Han clerical forms, with the rightward bend becoming established after the Eastern Han; its explanation that the bend helped distinguish 七 from 十 is a proposal.

One disputed account proposes that 七 first represented a word meaning “cut” and was then borrowed for the numeral, with 刀 added to write 切. This borrowing explanation depends on the words sounding alike or similarly, but no matched historical pronunciation pair for 七 and 切 is established in the supplied evidence.
A Han-period explanation interprets the graph through cosmological ideas of yang and yin. That historical interpretation does not independently establish what the earliest graph depicted.

uncertainties.text: The earliest graphic referent and its spoken name are not independently established. The cut interpretation and proposed borrowing sequence remain disputed, and the supplied evidence lacks a matched historical pronunciation pair for 七 and 切.

The transmitted Shijing text contains numeral uses, but the evidence does not establish the poem’s composition date or the date of its physical witness, so it does not settle the earliest surviving written attestation.

senses.period: Oracle-bone writing onward, as reported by a paleographic study
senses.text: A paleographic study reports 七 used for the numeral in oracle-bone writing and cites an oracle-bone example. This is an early attested numeral use; it does not rule out the disputed proposal of an earlier cut-related use.

senses.gloss: seven (Japanese readings なな and しち)
senses.period: Manyōshū example dated to the 8th century; later attestations also recorded
senses.text: Japanese lexical evidence records なな for “seven” in an 8th-century Manyōshū example and しち in an example from 1477. These Japanese readings and uses do not explain the origin of the Chinese graph.
A specialized Japanese sense meaning “gambler” is recorded with an example dated 1744. The evidence does not explain its development from “seven.”

limitations.text: The evidence supports early numeral use but does not settle whether it was the graph’s original meaning. It also gives no supported semantic path from “seven” to the later Japanese sense “gambler.”

overview.text: 七 means “seven,” and is documented for the numeral from oracle-bone writing onward. A disputed proposal says it was borrowed from a sign for cutting because the words may have sounded alike; that sound match is unconfirmed.

items.selection_reason: This clear early-script-style form illustrates the crossed shape documented in the numeral history, without treating the disputed “cut” interpretation as settled.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Pictogram (象形) – a vertical stroke and a horizontal stroke bisecting each other – original character of 切 (OC *sn̥ʰiːds, *sn̥ʰiːd, “to cut”).
The top-most horizontal stroke is done from left to right. The vertical stroke and bottom-most horizontal stroke are done as one stroke, from top-left to bottom-right.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *s-ni-s (“seven”).

evidence.source: Institute of History and Philology, Academia Sinica, 漢字「七」：字形演變
evidence.text: The entry identifies a bronze inscription and cites 集成04320, then proposes that 七 originally meant “cut,” that a short stroke was added across the horizontal stroke in bronze forms, and that the small-seal form bent the vertical stroke to distinguish it from 十. It says 七 was later borrowed for the numeral and 刀 was added to make 切. This is a source’s analysis, not a settled conclusion.
evidence.title: 漢字「七」：字形演變

evidence.source: Zhengzhou University Center for Research on Chinese Character Civilization, Chen Anqi
evidence.text: The study reports that 七 has recorded the numeral from oracle-bone writing through early Western Han clerical forms. It describes the early graph as crossed horizontal and vertical strokes, and says a bent lower vertical stroke appears after the Eastern Han. Its proposed explanation for the graphic change is avoidance of confusion with 十. The article cites specific examples, including oracle-bone 合集10650, Western Zhou 小盂鼎 inscription 集成2839, Qin Shuihudi slips, and Eastern Han-period Wuwei medical slips. It also discusses alternate spellings 桼、漆、柒 and copy or printing errors in those forms; these are numeral spellings, not necessarily stages in 七’s graphic development.
evidence.title: 数词{七}的用字研究（一）

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.text: The database says interpretations of 七’s shape are numerous and unresolved. It favors the analysis that 七 is an early form of 切: 一 and 丨 represent cutting across a line, and after 七 was borrowed for the numeral, 刀 was added to form 切. It also records a different proposal that the shape originated in a hand gesture. This supports reporting the cut analysis as a proposal rather than established graphic fact.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: Xu Shen, Shuowen Jiezi (as quoted in the CUHK character database and dossier)
evidence.text: The Shuowen explanation is 陽之正也。从一，微陰从中衺出也。凡七之屬皆从七. This is a Han-period cosmological interpretation of the graph; it does not independently establish the original graphic referent. The CUHK entry quotes it while noting competing interpretations.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: Institute of History and Natural Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences, 詩經·豳風·七月
evidence.text: The transmitted poem repeatedly uses 七 in calendrical and counting contexts, including 七月流火 and 七月食瓜. This establishes an early textual numeral use, but the page does not date the physical witness or by itself establish when the poem was composed. It is lexical evidence for the numeral, separate from claims about the graph’s original referent.
evidence.title: 诗经·豳风·七月

evidence.source: Kotobank, entry citing 精選版 日本国語大辞典 and 普及版 字通

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.

items.period: Shang oracle-script style (approx. 13th–11th century BCE convention; vector file uploaded 2011, revised 2018)
items.tradition: Oracle-bone script style; modern vector redraw
items.caption: A crossed horizontal and vertical form of 七, shown in a modern redraw labeled as Shang oracle script. A study cites oracle-bone examples of 七 used as the numeral seven.
items.alt: A black horizontal stroke crossed by a vertical stroke, with the vertical extending above and below, on a white square background.
items.selection_reason: This clear early-script-style form illustrates the crossed shape documented in the numeral history, without treating the disputed “cut” interpretation as settled.
items.rights: Commons file page states CC0 1.0 and attributes the pictured source to Xiaoxuetang; no artifact photograph is implied.

items.period: Qin/Han seal-script tradition represented by the Shuowen seal style (the SVG is a modern redraw, uploaded 2011 and revised 2018)
items.tradition: Small-seal script style; modern vector redraw
items.caption: A modern redraw of 七 in Shuowen seal-script style, with the lower part of its vertical stroke curving to the side.
items.alt: A black horizontal stroke crossed by a vertical stroke whose lower portion curves to the right, on a white square background.
items.selection_reason: It provides a useful comparison with the crossed form: one study reports that the lower stroke later bent right, while accounts differ on how to explain that change.
items.rights: Commons page identifies the Xiaoxuetang glyph image as CC0 1.0 and offers the file under CC0.

limitations.text: These images are modern redrawings of script styles, not photographs of ancient inscriptions. The early graph’s original referent remains uncertain: the proposal that it represented cutting is disputed, and the crossed form is also documented in numeral use.
